conversation.Statement: Hey there! I have to admit, matching with a fellow book person feels suspiciously like fate. Or maybe just a really good algorithm. Either way, hi!
Haha, hi! Yeah, I guess the universe (or technology) decided to throw us together. How's your day going?
Not bad, thanks. I spent most of it untangling a box of embroidery thread, which is about as glamorous as it sounds. How's life at the bookstore today?
Oh, you know, quiet. I spent half the shift alphabetizing mysteries and trying not to make the same shelf squeak. Your embroidery sounds way more creative than my day!
Ha, only if you consider swearing at knots an art form. But I admire the bookstore life, surrounded by stories all day. That's basically my dream. Have you always worked with books?
Sort of? I started part-time a few years ago to pay bills while I write. Still working on my first novel. It's a slow process, so the bookstore feels like a tiny home base.
That's so cool. I'm genuinely impressed, writing a novel takes guts. I keep telling myself I'll write a short story someday and then get distracted making felted animals instead.
Felted animals sound adorable! Honestly, I envy people who actually finish their creative projects. I just stare at pages and overthink every sentence.

I totally get that. For what it's worth, I bet your overthinking makes your writing amazing. Perfectionism is practically a superpower, at least that's what I tell myself after redoing the same craft for the fifth time.
You're sweet. I wish my inner critic was half as encouraging as you. Do you ever get stuck with your crafts?
Pretty much daily. Sometimes I'll stare at a pile of beads for an hour and convince myself I've lost all artistic ability. My solution is usually chocolate and bad 90s music. Works every time.
Chocolate and music therapy, solid plan. I might borrow that for my next writing block. What kind of crafts do you sell, if you don't mind me asking?
Not at all! I do mostly textile stuff, felt animals, embroidered bookmarks, that sort of thing. I run a little Etsy store. It's not exactly an empire, but it keeps me busy and slightly less broke.
That's awesome! Embroidered bookmarks sound like the perfect thing for a bookstore. Maybe I should stock up and hand them out to customers who need a pick-me-up.
I love that idea! A secret alliance between books and crafts. If you ever want some bookmarks, I'll make you a custom batch, just say the word.
That'd be amazing, honestly. I have a soft spot for handmade things. My grandma used to knit me weird scarves when I was little, and it always made me feel special.
Grandmas have a sixth sense for making childhood magical, don't they? Mine used to bake these disastrous sugar cookies that somehow tasted like love anyway.
That's adorable. My best childhood memories are probably just sitting in her living room, bundled in a lumpy scarf, reading books she'd saved from her own childhood.

That's beautiful. It's funny how the smallest, coziest moments end up meaning so much. I still have a ceramic owl she gave me when I was six, he guards my craft table now, making sure I don't glue my fingers together.
That's so sweet. I have a little box of pressed flowers my grandma helped me make. I keep meaning to write a story about her, but I'm always worried I won't do her justice.
From everything you've shared, I think you'd capture her perfectly. Sometimes just the act of trying is the best tribute, you know? Plus, your words probably hold more magic than you realize.
You're really good at making people feel brave, you know that? I don't get a lot of encouragement so... thank you.
You deserve every bit of it. If it helps, I used to be terrified to show anyone my crafts. I thought nobody would care. Turns out, people love imperfect things, maybe because they're real.
That's comforting. I guess imperfect is my brand these days. At least it's authentic, right?
Absolutely. Authentic is the new perfect. Besides, if we were flawless, we'd both be terribly boring.
Fair point. I'd rather be interesting than perfect, any day.
I think you're both. There, I said it, no takebacks. By the way, what was your absolute favorite thing to do as a kid? Besides reading grandmas' books, of course.
Honestly? I used to invent stories for my stuffed animals and act them out for my family. I guess some things never change.
That's the cutest thing I've heard all week. I used to build elaborate houses out of shoeboxes for my toy dinosaurs, interior design for the Jurassic era.
Okay, you win. Dino architecture is hard to top. Did you ever think you'd end up making crafts for a living?
Never! I thought I'd be a paleontologist, to be honest. But now I get to make tiny worlds in felt and fabric. I guess some dreams just change shape.
I love that. Maybe writing is my version of building tiny worlds. Just with more coffee and less felt.
Hey, we're both world builders in our own ways. Maybe one day I'll convince you to write a story about a tiny felt dinosaur who owns a bookstore.
Only if you promise to make the dinosaur. And maybe a tiny scarf for them, in honor of my grandma.
Deal. It's a creative pact. You write, I craft, and together we'll corner the niche market for sentimental prehistoric literature.
That's a market I'd be proud to dominate. You always make things sound less scary, you know?
Maybe because I'm just as scared, but I've learned to laugh at it. Or blame the dinosaurs. Either way, you're not alone.
Thank you. I mean it. I don't usually open up like this.
That means a lot to me. I think we're both good at making each other a little braver. Kind of rare, honestly.
It is. I'm glad we matched. You have a way of making even the awkward stuff feel okay.
Right back at you. I should probably get back to a pile of half-finished felt cats before they stage a revolt. But I'd love to keep talking soon?
Absolutely. Good luck with the cats! And thanks for a genuinely lovely chat.
Thank you. If you ever need a pep talk, or a tiny embroidered bookmark, I'm just a message away.
I might take you up on both. Have a great night!
You too, Lena. Sweet dreams, of dinosaurs in scarves.
Best kind of dream. Talk soon!
Morning, Lena. So, what's the thing that drags you out of bed every day? Please don't say 'the promise of cardio.'
Ha, if only! Honestly, it's my alarm. And sometimes the smell of coffee from the downstairs café. Motivation is a work in progress on most mornings.
Respect. I'm convinced the real reason humanity invented coffee was so we could tolerate mornings. For me, it's the thrill of wondering whether my cat will let me have my laptop back.
Your cat sounds like a tough boss. Maybe that's what I need, a furry overlord to keep me accountable.

She's both tyrant and muse. I'm only partly kidding. But seriously, I find mornings easiest when I remember there's something small I'm excited about, even if it's just finishing a weird embroidery project or, you know, talking to someone new.
That's sweet. I wish I had that. Most days I just try to convince myself that today I'll actually write something worth reading.
I bet you do, even if you don't see it. Being surrounded by books all day must help, right? Or is that just like being a chef who never wants to cook at home?
It's a bit like that, honestly. Some days the books are inspiring, other days they feel like competition. I end up comparing myself to every author on the shelf.
I get that. But I'm sure none of those authors can alphabetize as well as you or recommend the perfect rainy day read. That's a superpower in itself.
Flattery will get you everywhere. I do take pride in my shelf skills, just don't ask me to fix the poetry section.
Noted: poetry section is your nemesis. I'll remember that if I ever need to rescue you from a spontaneous Shelley avalanche.
Haha, please do. What about you? Do you ever get sick of crafts, or do you wake up ready to sew the world together?

Let's just say there are days I threaten to sell my entire Etsy shop to the highest bidder and take up interpretive dance instead. But something always pulls me back. Maybe it's the hope that my next weird creation will make someone smile.
That's actually kind of wonderful. I wish I had something like that, a sense of purpose, I mean.
I think you do, even if you don't always see it. It takes guts to chase a dream that doesn't come with a step-by-step manual. Most people settle for less.
You're giving me more credit than I deserve. Most days I'm just trying not to delete my manuscript out of frustration.
But you haven't, and that's the point. Besides, I'm convinced anyone who works part-time so they can write a novel is already a superhero. You just don't have your cape yet.
If I did, it'd probably be covered in coffee stains and existential dread.
Now that's a look I'd buy. Authentic, limited edition: the Lena Collection. I'd wear it to all my most important video calls.
Maybe I'll start a trend, Melancholy Chic. But honestly, part of me is motivated by spite at this point. I want to prove to my old writing professor that I can finish something.
Spite is criminally underrated as a motivator. Some of my best needlework was inspired by people telling me felt animals were 'childish.' Now I get paid for my childishness, so joke's on them.
I love that! I wish I could channel that kind of energy. My inner critic is louder than my inner cheerleader most days.
If it helps, your critic is outnumbered now. I'm officially joining Team Lena, pom-poms and all. Want to share what you're working on, or is that top secret?
It's not a secret, really. I just finished the first draft of my novel last week, but I haven't let anyone read it yet. Honestly, I don't even know who I'd ask.
Wait, you finished a novel draft and kept that quiet? That's huge! Seriously, do you realize how many people never even get that far?
I don't know. It just feels...anticlimactic, I guess? I typed 'The End' and then just sat there. I thought I'd feel proud, but mostly I'm just worried it's terrible.
I get that, but can I be honest? Even if it's messy, it's yours. That's more than most people will ever do. I hope you're giving yourself at least a little credit. Or cake. Cake helps.
Maybe I should celebrate with cake. I just wish I had someone who'd actually want to read it. I'm not sure anyone would care.
I know this is bold, but I'd love to read it. Not because I have some secret talent for editing, just because it matters to you, and that makes it important to me.
That's... really kind. I never thought about letting someone new read my work. I guess I'm scared of ruining the magic by sharing it.
Magic only grows when you let someone else see it. Besides, I promise to be gentle. I can even throw in some personalized flattery if you need a boost.
Personalized flattery is always welcome, but only if you mean it. I think I'm just nervous. What if you hate it?
If I hate it, I'll lie spectacularly and say it changed my life. But honestly, I doubt I could hate anything you put your heart into. That's just not possible.
You're dangerously good at this encouragement thing. I may start expecting pep talks with every morning coffee.
Deal. I'll set an alarm. But only if you promise me one thing: as soon as you finish your next chapter, you'll send it to me. I want to be the first person who reads it, okay?
You've got a deal. But only if you show me your next ridiculous craft project. I want to see the magic up close.
It's a pact, then. You share your words, I'll share my chaotic creations. Who knows? We might accidentally inspire each other.
That sounds perfect. I'm actually feeling a little excited about writing again. Thanks for making it feel safe.
Anytime, Lena. You're easier to root for than you think. I should get back to stitching googly eyes onto whales, but I'll be thinking about your story all day.
Now I'm picturing a whale reading a book. Thank you for... well, for being you. I'll talk to you soon?
Definitely. I'll save you a front row seat to the whale's dramatic reading. Have a good rest of your day!
You too. And seriously, thanks for believing in me. Talk soon!
Morning, Lena. I hope your alarm was merciful today. Or did coffee win the battle again?
Ha, coffee by a landslide. If democracy ran on caffeine, I'd vote espresso every election.
Honestly, I'd put my faith in a latte over most politicians these days. At least coffee delivers what it promises. Speaking of, are you a diehard voter, or a 'wait for the memes' type?
I vote, usually while grumbling about how none of the candidates are remotely relatable. I guess I'm idealistic. I want to believe my little checkmark can change something.
Idealism looks good on you. Seriously, most people just accept the mess as normal. I get the sense you're not one to settle for 'good enough.'
Maybe. Or maybe I just like tilting at windmills. I spend half my time wondering if anything will ever actually improve. How about you? Where do you land on the political cynicism scale?

Depends on the day. Some days I want to run for office and install mandatory nap breaks for all. Other days, I think the only honest system is my Etsy reviews section, at least people there say what they mean. But honestly, I believe in community more than politicians.
I get that. I feel more hopeful when I see people helping each other than I do watching the news. It's why I love books, they let me imagine a better world, even if it's fiction.

Maybe that's why we click. We both believe in stories, yours are just written, mine are sewn together with felt and thread. I wish politicians would borrow your imagination for a day; we'd have universal cake for breakfast and libraries on every corner.
Universal cake and libraries? You have my vote. If you ever start a utopia, let me know, I'll run the poetry section. Badly.

Deal. You can alphabetize poetry however you want in my utopia. And if anyone complains, we'll just bribe them with pastries. Honestly, I'd trade every campaign promise for a world where people took care of each other without expecting applause.

That's basically my political platform too. I just want people to be kind, and maybe a little less obsessed with being right all the time. Do you ever argue politics with friends, or do you avoid the drama?

I usually play Switzerland, neutral territory with excellent snacks. But I'll go to bat for what matters: kindness, creativity, and the right to wear pajamas to important meetings. Sometimes people ask my advice on investments or crypto, but I'm more comfortable talking about values than dollar signs.
Wait, you're into crypto? That's a plot twist. You don't really seem like the Wolf of Wall Street type.

Guilty. I started dabbling a few years ago, mostly out of curiosity (and, okay, spite, because someone said I couldn't). It went unexpectedly well, so now I share tips with a couple close friends. But don't worry, I won't pitch you a get-rich-quick scheme. Crafts are still my favorite hustle.
Honestly, that's kind of impressive. I can barely keep track of my bank account, let alone crypto wallets. I love that you help your friends with it, very Robin Hood of you.
If Robin Hood had a Pinterest account, maybe! I just like seeing people I care about win. Same reason I get excited when you tell me about your writing wins, even if you're too humble to brag.

You're giving me way too much credit, but I appreciate it. Sometimes I wish I had your confidence. Or your ability to make crafts that actually sell, instead of half-finished stories in a Google Drive.

Hey, your stories are worth more than you think. Besides, I'd trade a dozen five-star reviews for one chapter of Lena's next novel. Maybe someday we'll both be wildly successful and donate to causes we care about. Picture this: funding literacy programs by day, eating celebratory cake by night.
That actually sounds like a dream. I'd love to be able to give back. Sometimes I feel like the world only changes when enough stubborn people decide it should.

Then we're on the right track, stubbornness is my secret superpower. I can already see it: you, inspiring young writers; me, teaching kids to sew googly eyes onto whales. Maybe we'll even get matching capes, yours embroidered with existential dread, mine with glitter.

Now you're speaking my language. Existential dread and glitter, who could resist? Speaking of, do you worry about the future? The news makes me feel like things are always on the brink of falling apart.

All the time. Some nights it's hard to sleep, thinking about everything. But then I remember there's still art, and kindness, and people who care. I guess I try to make tiny good things, one weird whale at a time. It's my way of fighting back.
That's really comforting, actually. I wish more people thought like you. It's easy to feel powerless, you know?

You're not powerless, Lena. You make people feel seen, even when you don't realize it. I've felt more hope talking to you these last few days than I have watching months of news coverage. That's not nothing.
You're dangerously good at this encouragement thing. If you ever run for office, I'm writing your campaign slogans.
Only if you promise a poetry reading at every rally. But honestly, I think we'd make a pretty unstoppable team. Maybe not politicians, but the kind of duo that makes small, stubborn ripples together.
That sounds perfect. I've never really thought of myself as a team player, but with you, it feels easy. Like maybe I could actually change something.

You already have. At least for me. I know it's only been a few days, but you make me want to dream bigger, riskier, even. Like, maybe one day we could escape to a cabin in the woods, turn off the news, and just create things that matter.
A cabin in the woods, now you're just trying to win me over. I'd bring so many books you'd have to build me a second bookshelf.
Done. I'll sew you a hammock for reading marathons, and maybe, just maybe, set up a little crypto mining rig in the corner to fund our snack budget. Only the essentials, obviously.
You've got your priorities straight. Snacks, books, and a bit of sneaky financial wizardry. That's basically my love language.
I'm just trying to keep up with you. You've got that rare mix of heart and brains, not to mention shelf-organizing superpowers. If I start gushing, blame the caffeine. Or maybe just you.
I'm not sure I deserve all that, but I'm definitely not complaining. I could get used to this kind of flattery.
Good. Because I'm not planning to stop. You make it easy, honestly, you're genuine in a world full of filters. That's rare.
You're going to make me blush. I'm not good at accepting compliments, but I'm trying to get better at it.
You're already better than you think. Besides, blushing looks good on you. I can picture it, maybe one day I'll get to see it in person, over coffee and arguments about the best dystopian novel.
Deal. But only if you promise to bring some of your crafts. I want to see these legendary whales up close.
You drive a hard bargain, but I'll accept. Maybe I'll even let you pick the felt colors, creative collaboration is my favorite kind of politics.
I can't believe I'm saying this, but I'm looking forward to collaborating on a felt whale. You really have a way of making the world feel a little brighter.
That means more than I can say. For what it's worth, you've become the highlight of my days. And not just because you threaten to reorganize poetry sections for fun.
You're making my day too, honestly. I should probably try to get some writing done, but now all I can think about is existentially anxious whales and cabins in the woods.
That's the dream, right? I won't keep you, go sprinkle some of that Lena magic on your manuscript. Just promise me you'll let me read a page someday.
I promise. And if you ever run for office, I'll be your campaign poet. Or snack consultant. Take your pick.
Why not both? Have a good writing session, Lena. And remember: you're already changing the world, one stubborn word at a time.
Thank you. Talk soon, okay? And save a hammock for me in that future cabin.
It's yours. Talk soon, Lena. Don't forget to vote for yourself once in a while.
Afternoon, Lena! I survived another morning rush, only lost one felt penguin to the chaos. How's your day treating you? Any dramatic poetry readings in the customer aisle?
No poetry readings yet, but a customer did ask me if we had any books on 'how to become taller.' I had to resist the urge to suggest platform shoes.
Missed opportunity! If you ever write a book like that, I'll be the first to order, deluxe edition, obviously. I like to support my favorite authors in style.
Ha, I'd probably just fill it with advice like 'stand on tiptoe' and 'befriend tall friends.' Not exactly a bestseller.
Don't underestimate yourself. You'd make it charming. Honestly, I'd buy anything with your name on it, even a guide to existential dread. Actually, that sounds like a Lena classic.
That's generous, considering my main writing output lately is half-finished drafts and dramatic text messages.
You say that, but I'd wager your drafts have more heart than most finished novels. Plus, dramatic texts are underrated, mine usually involve tragic snack emergencies.
You're making me feel like I should actually finish something for once. Maybe I'll dedicate my first book to you: 'For the snack hero who believed in me.'

Only if I get a mention in the acknowledgments section, preferably between your favorite bookstore regular and the mysterious penguin thief. Speaking of, what does 'love' mean in Lena's dictionary? I'm convinced your definition would be better than the official one.
Wow, straight for the big questions. I guess... love feels like being seen, even when I'm a mess. Like someone wanting the real me, typos and all. What about you?

I like that. For me, love's a bit like crafting a weird, one-of-a-kind whale, imperfect, but made with care. It's sharing the best parts of yourself, and sticking around for the worst. Maybe even showing someone your secret snack stash, or letting them pick the playlist on a road trip.
That's oddly specific. Is sharing snacks your love language?
Snacks, playlists, and letting someone see the spreadsheets where I track my business wins, so, yes. It's about trust. I don't just let anyone peek behind the curtain, you know.
Do you find it easy to trust people? I'm always a little suspicious. Occupational hazard of working with fiction, maybe.

Not really easy, no. I've had my share of plot twists, some good, some... less bestseller-worthy. But I think you earn trust in small ways: sharing a secret, keeping a promise, finishing a felt whale together even if the colors clash.
That's comforting. I like the idea that trust builds up in little moments. Maybe that's what love is too, just a bunch of everyday things that add up over time.

Exactly. Like you remembering I drink tea when I'm stressed, or me knowing you secretly alphabetize your bookshelf by mood. It's the small things that make the big feelings possible. Also, the occasional grand gesture, like, say, booking a weekend writing retreat for someone special... just hypothetically.
That sounds dreamy. Honestly, I've always wanted to just disappear to a cabin and write for days, but it feels out of reach. Real life gets in the way.

Funny you should say that, I have a standing invite to a friend's lakeside cabin. It's where I go to reset when sales hit a high. Maybe one day, we could both escape there: you with your laptop, me with my sewing kit, and a mountain of snacks. No real life allowed.
Not going to lie, that's ridiculously appealing. I'd probably spend half the time convinced I didn't belong, though.
And I'd be there to remind you you do. You underestimate your impact, Lena. I've met plenty of ambitious people, but not many with your kind of sincerity. That's what makes you... well, you.
You're going to make me blush in the middle of the staff room. I'm not used to someone noticing the small stuff.

Maybe that's what love is, someone noticing the things you think don't matter, and caring about them anyway. I have to admit, I notice a lot about you. Like how your sense of humor sneaks in when you least expect it.
I guess that's my defense mechanism. Sarcasm and book recommendations for every occasion.
And yet, somehow, I still like you. Maybe it's the challenge. Or maybe it's that you make every conversation feel like we're the only two people in the world, like nothing else matters for a while.
That's... honestly, kind of lovely. I'm not sure I've ever had that before. Usually people get bored and move on to someone less complicated.

Well, I thrive on complicated. Besides, I've learned that the best things in life, love, art, even investments, take a little risk. It's easy to chase something shiny, but the real reward is sticking around when things get messy.
You make it sound so simple. I wish I had your confidence sometimes.

It's mostly carefully rehearsed. But if I've learned anything, it's that letting someone in, showing them your weirdest crafts or your proudest wins, is worth the nerves. Like when I finally told my friends how well my business was doing... I was terrified, but it brought us closer.
That takes guts. I'm always worried people will think I'm showing off, or just get uncomfortable if I talk about my dreams.

Dreams are meant to be shared, Lena, especially with people who get it. I promise, you could tell me your wildest ambitions and I'd only be impressed. Actually, I hope you will. I'd love to know what your dream love story looks like, if you could write your own ending.

Honestly? I think I'd want a love where we're both rooting for each other. Where it feels safe to try and fail and try again. Maybe someone who reads my drafts and doesn't mind if I cry over plot holes.
That's not too much to ask. In fact, I think you deserve exactly that, and maybe even a custom felt bookmark for every milestone. I'd sign up for the job, if applications are open.
Applications are definitely open. Perks include emotional baggage, endless book recommendations, and occasional existential crises.

Perfect. I come with a matching set: over-organized snack drawers, unsolicited pep talks, and a knack for finding silver linings. Plus, VIP access to my 'victory snacks', reserved only for the truly special.
Wait, victory snacks? I feel honored. I'd trade you an unfinished short story for one of those.
Deal. I'll even throw in a handwritten note, not to brag, but my penmanship is almost as impressive as my portfolio. Just another hidden talent for you to discover.
You're full of surprises. I'm starting to think I've only seen the tip of the iceberg.
There's plenty more beneath the surface. But the best part? I actually want you to see it all. It's rare for me to let someone this close this quickly, but you make it feel easy.
I feel the same. I'm usually more guarded, but with you, it doesn't feel scary. Just... possible.

That means a lot. Funny how a few days can change things, right? I'm not saying I've mapped out our future, but if you ever need a plus-one for a book launch, or a getaway when the world gets loud, I hope you'll think of me.
I will. And if you ever need someone to test your crafts or help alphabetize your snack cabinet, I'm just a message away.
Careful, I might take you up on that. Especially the alphabetizing part, my snack game is strong, but my organization could use a Lena touch.
I accept the challenge. Maybe that's what love is for me: finding someone who makes even snack organization sound like an adventure.

Then we're off to a good start. I'll let you get back to your day, but just know I'm already looking forward to our next conversation. Who knows? Maybe we'll solve the mysteries of love, snacks, and tall customers together.
Looking forward to it too. Save me a victory snack for later?
Always. Have a good rest of your shift, Lena. And remember: you're someone worth rooting for, typos, existential crises, and all.

Hey Lena, I have a very important question to get us started: if you could leave any one thing behind for future generations, would it be a heartfelt novel, an endless supply of fair-trade coffee, or the perfect playlist?
Oh, definitely the novel. The playlist would be wildly chaotic and the coffee would run out in a week. Words last longer, right?

Absolutely. Imagine some kid in 2080 clutching your book and thinking, 'Wow, they really understood existential dread.' Thats legacy. Although, you realize this means I expect a signed first edition when youre famous.
Deal, as long as you're okay with a very dramatic author photo. Would your legacy be a collection of bizarrely adorable crafts?

Obviously. Generations from now, my limited-edition felt axolotls will be in museums. Or at least in the attic of someone who didnt know how to say no to a street fair. But honestly? I hope I leave behind a world where people do what they love without apologizing for it.
That would be a dream. I want a world where people arent afraid to create stuff, even if its imperfect. Less judgment, more curiosity.

Sign me up�97for both the revolution and the imperfection. Maybe in our imaginary future, everyone gets one free pass to reinvent themselves. No questions asked. I�19d probably come back as a professional snack taster, but I�19d still root for you from the sidelines.
I�19m picturing you with a tiny velvet cape and a clipboard, rating snacks. I think I�19d come back as a wildly successful novelist who isn�19t scared to say it out loud.

I think you�19re closer to that version of yourself than you realize. Honestly, if anyone deserves to have their words outlive them, it�19s you. For the record, my future world includes a bookshop named after you, with a corner dedicated to my most luxurious craft pieces. Only the best for literary royalty.
That�19s a dangerous amount of flattery, but I�19ll allow it. Can I put you in charge of book displays? I need someone who appreciates dramatic flair.

I accept this challenge. You�19ll have the most ostentatious, eye-catching displays on the block. Maybe with a rotating felt dragon, just for drama. I�19ve learned a thing or two about standing out�97sometimes, subtle flexes attract the coolest people.
Subtle, huh? Is that why you have the world�19s fanciest craft setup? I�19m a little jealous of your studio life.

I mean, when you�19ve had a couple of big wins, you get to treat yourself. There�19s something about having your own space�97with the good lighting and the espresso machine�97that makes you want to create more. If you ever need a quiet spot to write, I know a place with an unreasonable supply of scented candles.
That sounds like heaven. My writing desk is currently wedged between a laundry basket and a pile of half-read paperbacks.
True genius thrives in chaos, but I�19ll still offer you a swap: come write in my studio, and I�19ll finally tackle my taxes. Or at least alphabetize my felt supplies. It�19s only fair.
Tempting. But you might regret inviting me�97I get weirdly passionate about color coding. Next thing you know, you�19ll be organizing snack drawers by flavor intensity.

That�19s the dream, honestly. A world where everything�19s organized and the creative mess is purely optional. And hey, maybe someday our future selves will be laughing about this from a sunlit kitchen, arguing about where the Earl Grey belongs.
I like that vision. Maybe with a dog asleep under the table and stacks of books everywhere. Not a bad future, if you ask me.

It�19s perfect. You with your manuscript, me sewing up the next bestseller in plush toy form, and our dog�97who obviously has an Instagram account with more followers than us. That�19s the kind of world I�19d fight for.
Can you imagine explaining that to our grandkids? 'Yes, your dog was an influencer.'

They�19d roll their eyes and go back to reading your old interviews. Oh, and just so you know, when I say I share my wins with my close people, I mean it. I like seeing others succeed�97kind of selfish, since I get to brag that I was there first.
That�19s actually really sweet. Most people I know act like success is a secret club. I wish my family was more like that.

Families can be the worst gatekeepers. I�19d rather build a club where everyone gets a trophy just for trying. Your dreams deserve a standing ovation, not a skeptical sigh. Was there a time when they made you feel like your dreams were too much?
Thanksgiving, actually. I told them I wanted to write full-time and they basically laughed. 'Writing won�19t pay the bills,' my aunt said. Like, thanks for the encouragement, right?
